rv.q: Rufus Norris, the National’s outgoing artistic director, deserves a big hit and this is it.
The play is thrillingly directed by Rufus Norris with inventive designs and a stage that’s teeming.
Rufus Norris and his creative team attain a pulse-quickening theatricality, the ensemble as tightly drilled as an A&E team...
Throughout it all, Sheen burns with genuine passion.
This is, unashamedly, a play about principle, passion and compassion, driven by a fantastic ensemble and an electrifying performance from Sheen.

And there’s no sense of embarrassment from Sheen, who is magnetic as Bevan - a decent, even slightly bewildered man, who nonetheless feels pathologically drawn to doing the right thing, no matter the odds.
Imperfect, but stirringly impassioned.
Bevan’s exceptionalism shines through, but with so much history to cover the show feels skimpy at times.

Writer Tim Price and outgoing National Theatre artistic director Rufus Norris have turned this welfare state origin story into a weird, sometimes baggy reverie, enlivened with poignant biographical insights.
Nye is a too full, yet too simplified, survey of the personal and political elements in Bevan’s world, with some high-pitched moments accompanied by syrupy music.
But Price is so keen to beatify Bevan that his exemplary life passes almost unopposed.

In the theatrical equivalent of the nervous giggle that overtakes someone on hearing bad news, Rufus Norris’s production is infected with a dreadful larkiness, which goes beyond conveying the weirdness of fever.
Tim Price’s new play is not perfect, but, my word, it is passionate, burning with excitement, joy, despair and fury, with a firebrand style that perfectly suits its subject matter.
Michael Sheen, in the part he was surely born to play, is on stage throughout, carrying the play and the man with equal passion.
The whole company maintain the rapid flow of Rufus Norris’s production and Steven Hoggett and Jess Williams choreography, with Vicki Mortimer’s simple setting suddenly erupting into spectacle.
Each scene is entertaining, but there is no overarching style to give the show a solid and coherent identity.
It’s engaging, never less than interesting, but it doesn’t always find the balance between great gobbets of historical information and reaching the heart of the man and his vision.
Nye’s story deserves to echo through the ages.
Nye is, on the whole, a magnificent celebration of our NHS and the man behind it...
The result is a moving but unsentimental portrait of the man who changed British healthcare.
It’s a workmanlike history play at a time of anxiety about the great service itself.

Excellent direction and a fantastically strong performance from Michael Sheen alongside an equally impressive cast ensure there is still much to love about Nye - it is just frustrating it never quite meets its potential as a whole.
Tim Price's uneven biodrama of socialist firebrand Nye Bevan offers most of an explanation - while failing to get under its subject's skin.

cn.t: Sheen delivers a charismatic performance as NHS founder Nye Bevan, but critics find Price's morphine-dream biography uneven—praised for ambition and staging, yet faulted for being overstuffed with detail and lacking emotional depth.

vr.q: It's a magnetic and moving performance.
